1:
The chapter opens with a delegation rather than a decree. reformed Gill sets the moment precisely: the land had been divided, every tribe now knew what belonged to it and what it could spare, and the six cities of refuge were fixed — only then did the Levites come forward to claim the towns they were to live in, having received no share in the division. The men who came were the principal men among them, the living heads of the three houses descended from Kohath, Gershon and Merari, a point Wesley makes in the same wesleyan-arminian terms: the fathers of the Levites were those three, and the heads were the chief persons then alive.

Matthew Henry, reading it as a puritan-evangelical pastor, fixes on two features of the petition. The first is what it rests on. The Levites do not plead service or merit; they plead a command — that the LORD had ordered by the hand of Moses that they be given cities, an order laid on Israel to grant and therefore on the Levites to ask. Henry presses the application hard: the maintenance of ministers is not an arbitrary thing left to the good-will of a people who may starve them if they please. As the God of Israel commanded that the Levites be provided for, so the King of the Christian church has ordained that those who preach the gospel should live of the gospel, and live comfortably, and Henry anchors it in 1 Corinthians 9:14.

The second feature is the timing, and Henry will not let it pass as accident. The Levites waited until every other tribe was served. Part of the reason was practical — each tribe had to know its own before it could know what it was giving — but Henry reads modesty and patience in it too, and turns it on ministers who find themselves last in other men's thoughts: let them secure the favour of God and the honour that comes from him, and they can afford the neglect of men.

Calvin's reformed comment runs on the narrative order. He observes that this account belongs earlier than its place, since no cities of refuge could be appointed before the Levites had been assigned their towns, and since the land was not truly divided until the Levites were housed. His judgment on the delay is blunt and unflattering to Israel: it was disgraceful that the people needed pulling by the ear and reminding of what God had plainly ordered. Had the Levites not asked, there was a risk of their being left in the open air. Calvin softens it only so far — the fault looks like carelessness and forgetfulness rather than intent to defraud, since the people made no delay once admonished, and are praised for doing what was right according to the word of the LORD.

Clarke, writing from the wesleyan-arminian side, lays out the administrative shape: the Levites were three great families, with the house of Aaron forming in effect a fourth, and to none of them had God assigned any portion in the division. The intention throughout was that the tribes would furnish them habitations, by the positive command of Numbers 35:2 — so with every tribe's inheritance now settled, the heads of the Levites came before Eleazar, Joshua and the chiefs who had done the dividing, and asked for cities and their suburbs.
2:
The place matters to Gill, and he says why: Shiloh in the land of Canaan is where the tabernacle was fixed, and it was at or near the tabernacle that the men had met to cast lots for the seven tribes still without an inheritance. The Levites make their request where the lot was already being drawn, which is to say they ask at exactly the point where the answer could be given.

The request itself is quoted rather than paraphrased in the grammatical-historical notes of Keil and Delitzsch, who take verses 2 to 4 together as one administrative unit: the LORD commanded by the hand of Moses to give cities to dwell in, with their suburbs for cattle; Israel gave them out of its own inheritance at the commandment of the LORD; and the lot came out first for the Kohathites. Keil and Delitzsch then set out the family structure that governs the whole distribution — Levi divided into Gershonites, Kohathites and Merarites, with the Kohathites subdivided into the four houses of Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and the house of Amram into the two lines of Moses and Aaron, the priesthood falling to Aaron's.

Wesley takes the same clause and drives it where Henry drove it. The words to weigh are the Lord commanded. The provision for those who serve at the altar is not left to the goodwill of the people; as the God of Israel commanded that the Levites be provided for, so the Lord Jesus ordained — and Wesley calls it a perpetual ordinance — that they who preach the gospel should live of the gospel. Two witnesses of very different temper arrive at the same reading of the verse, and both take the imperative as binding beyond its original occasion.

What holds the verse together is that the claim is not framed as a grievance. The Levites do not accuse Israel of having forgotten them, though Calvin thought Israel had. They recite the command, name what it entitles them to — cities to dwell in, and pasture for the cattle that were their only property — and leave the rest to men who had the authority to act.
3:
Israel's answer takes one verse and no argument. Gill notes that the children of Israel knew full well there was such a command, made no objection to the motion, and freely gave cities out of the portion allotted to them. The freedom is the point: the towns came from inheritances already assigned, so every grant was a subtraction from something a tribe had just received.

Clarke reads obedience in it and adds the mechanism. They cheerfully obeyed the divine command, and the cities were appointed to the Levites by lot out of the different tribes — so that it might as fully appear that God designed the Levites their habitations as he had designed the other tribes their inheritances. The lot puts the distribution beyond negotiation and beyond gratitude; the Levites hold their towns by the same warrant the others hold their land.

Wesley works out the administrative sequence more finely. His suggestion is that the people gave such cities as God commanded without at first specifying which family got which, and that the lot then appropriated them to the several houses. He also presses out of their inheritance — that is, out of their several possessions, so the burden fell evenly across the tribes rather than on one. And he draws out the purpose in the dispersion itself: the Levites scattered among the tribes, as Jacob's word in Genesis 49:7 had foretold, could more easily and effectually teach Israel God's law and judgments, which was the charge laid on them in Deuteronomy 33:10, and the people could resort to them and ask the meaning of the law at their mouths.

On suburbs Wesley is careful, because a later dispute turns on it. What the Levites received was not merely the use of the ground but the absolute dominion of it. He argues this from two directions. The distinction drawn later in the chapter between the city and suburbs of Hebron, given to the Levites, and the fields and villages of Hebron, given to Caleb, only makes sense if the two were held on different terms; and the return of these cities to the Levites at the Jubilee, as their proper owners under Leviticus 25:33, settles the question of ownership rather than tenancy.
4:
The first lot falls to Kohath, and within Kohath to the sons of Aaron. Gill marks it simply — the first lot drawn out of the urn was for the descendants of Kohath, a son of Levi — and Keil and Delitzsch fill in the consequence in grammatical-historical detail: the priests received thirteen towns from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, while the rest of the Kohathites, the lines of Moses, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, received ten from Ephraim, Dan and half Manasseh; the Gershonites thirteen from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and half Manasseh in Bashan; the Merarites twelve from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun.

The interesting question is why the priests should have drawn the three tribes they did, and here Calvin is quoted inside Keil and Delitzsch's own comment and then develops the thought himself. This did not happen by chance; God in his admirable counsel placed the priests in the locality where he had determined to choose a temple for himself. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the other end, by administration rather than by decree: the part of the tribe whose business was to minister at the sanctuary, and the sanctuary was afterwards to be established at Jerusalem, had its appointment nearest that city, so that they were always within reach of the sacred work God had given them.

Clarke also explains the unequal shares by the rule that produced them. Judah, Simeon and Benjamin furnished more habitations in proportion than the other tribes because they possessed a larger inheritance, and Moses had commanded in Numbers 35:8 that from those who have many, many should be given, and from those who have few, few — each giving of his cities according to his inheritance.

Calvin then meets an objection head on. If the priests were destined for Jerusalem, why was Jerusalem not the first city given them? His answer has several parts. Moderate-sized cities were delivered to them as their condition required; Jerusalem was not then subjugated, remaining under the Jebusites; and it would in any case have been absurd to assign a royal seat to priests. Calvin turns the arrangement into evidence of their faith — no priest performed his office without becoming a stranger, since each migrated of his own accord from his native soil to attend to sacred things — while allowing that their weakness was indulged so far as to give them neighbouring cities, sparing them a long journey to their function. He closes with an inference he will repeat: thirteen cities for one family, and not a numerous one, confirms that the other tribes held many more cities than are actually named.

Wesley adds the forward-looking note. The priests were few enough at that moment for a single city, but the division was made for all future generations, and respect had to be paid to their coming numbers. Since a Levite might sell a house until the Jubilee under Leviticus 25:33, he could certainly let it; so Wesley judges the cities were not long half-empty, filled out by kinsmen and by those who wished to live near the service of God for the good of their souls.
5:
Two words carry this verse: the rest. Gill defines them by exclusion — the Kohathites who did not descend through Amram and Aaron, but through Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and who were therefore Levites and not priests. Clarke says the same thing in reverse, that this is the part of Kohath's family that were simply Levites, the priests among them having already had their lot in the preceding tribes. Their ten towns came from Ephraim, Dan and half Manasseh, and Wesley points out that these tribes lay nearest the three that had supplied the priests, so the Kohathite Levites were placed next to their Aaronite brethren; their share was smaller than the priests' because the inheritance they were drawn from was smaller.

Clarke then raises the question that hangs over the whole chapter, and answers it at length: in what sense did the Levites possess cities, when they had no inheritance? His conclusion is that they had no exclusive property in the towns they lived in, since other Israelites plainly lived there too. He cites Calmet for the general point that the Levitical cities were almost entirely filled with Israelites of other tribes, and then argues from cases. Gibeah of Benjamin, given to the Levites later in this chapter, was always peopled by Benjamites, as the narrative of the Levite and his wife in Judges 19:22 shows; Saul and all his house lived there. David and his court spent the first years of his reign at Hebron, itself a Levitical city.

What the Levites held, on Clarke's reading, was a right to certain houses, which they might sell but never finally alienate, since the right of redemption was perpetual and an unredeemed house reverted to the Levites at the Jubilee. The pasture ground reaching two thousand cubits outside the city they could not sell at all; it was reckoned the LORD's property, under Leviticus 25:32. Clarke's picture of the original settlement follows from this: the Levites chose the houses they would live in, and the men of the tribe occupied the rest, with more dwellings assigned as Levite families grew, probably built at public expense.

Nor were they confined to these towns. Clarke notes priests and Levites living at Nob when the tabernacle stood there, in 1 Samuel 21:1; multitudes of both at Jerusalem once the worship of God was established there, though Jerusalem was no Levitical city; and courses of priests afterwards at Jericho. He takes this to be a circumstance Moses had foreseen and provided for in Deuteronomy 18:6.
6:
Gershon was Levi's eldest son, and his descendants are placed third. Gill records the fact without comment on the order — these were Levites descended from Gershon, and their cities were assigned by lot in tribes lying at a greater distance, not only Issachar but Asher, Naphtali and half Manasseh in Bashan. Keil and Delitzsch give the tally: thirteen towns.

Their grammatical-historical interest lies in whether the number is credible, and they take the objection seriously enough to answer it in three parts. Judging by how many towns a land that size held, most of them cannot have been very large. The Levites were not the sole possessors of the towns in any case, but received the dwelling-houses they actually needed, with meadow land for their cattle in the suburbs, the rest of the space still belonging to the tribe. And the arithmetic works: if the twenty-three thousand males counted at the second census in the steppes of Moab were distributed across the thirty-five towns that fell to the non-priestly Levites, that is roughly six hundred and fifty males, or something like thirteen hundred Levites of both sexes, to a town.

The effect of the calculation is to turn a figure that looks extravagant into one that looks modest. Forty-eight towns for the smallest tribe reads as generosity until the towns are measured and the population divided into them; then it reads as sufficiency. The point will be made again at the close of the list, where Calvin and Wesley both return to it from different angles.

Gill's own emphasis falls on distance. The Gershonites, descending from Levi's eldest son, had their cities assigned in tribes lying further off — Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half tribe of Manasseh in Bashan — which puts the senior house of Levi at the northern edge of the settlement while the junior Kohathites hold the centre. Nothing in the text treats this as a slight, and the lot rather than any man's preference produced it.

The census figure Keil and Delitzsch use comes from the second numbering in the plains of Moab, and the way they handle it is characteristic of their method: an objection about plausibility is answered with arithmetic and with the legal terms of the grant rather than with assertion. Since the Levites received dwelling-houses and pasture and not the towns entire, the question is never how many people forty-eight whole towns would hold, but how many households the Levites actually needed to place.
7:
Merari, Levi's third son, comes last and receives least. Gill identifies the family and leaves it there; Keil and Delitzsch record twelve towns from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun, and use the moment to continue the defence of the whole scheme's proportions that they began at the previous verse.

Their argument is worth following because it governs how the rest of the chapter should be read. The towns were mostly small. The Levites did not own them outright but held the houses they needed, with pasture in the suburbs, the remainder of the ground staying with the tribe. And the census figure of twenty-three thousand Levite males, spread across the towns, gives a population per town that no one would call crowded.

Keil and Delitzsch then raise the harder objection, the one about the priests specifically: thirteen towns handed over to the sons of Aaron looks disproportionate when Aaron himself left only two sons. Their answer is the one Wesley reaches independently — the provision was made for generations, not for a moment. The distribution had to serve a priesthood that would in time be numbered in courses, and a grant sized to the family as it stood at Shiloh would have been useless within a century.

Reading the three lots together, an order emerges that the text does not comment on but does observe. The priests are placed around the future sanctuary; the remaining Kohathites next to them; Gershon, though the eldest house, after the younger Kohathites; and Merari furthest out, across the Jordan and in the north.

Gill's identification is the barest possible — the descendants of Merari, the third son of Levi — but the placement it introduces is not trivial. Reuben and Gad lay east of the Jordan and Zebulun in the north, so the youngest Levite house was distributed furthest from the sanctuary the priests were gathered around. The four lots read, laid end to end, as a series of concentric rings.

Keil and Delitzsch's defence of the numbers is a single argument in three movements, and it is directed at a real objection rather than an imagined one. Commentators had taken offence at the scale of the grant. The reply is that the towns were small, that the grant conveyed houses and pasture rather than territory, and that the Levite population divided into the towns yields nothing extravagant. Their further note about the priests' thirteen towns — that the figure looks impossible if Aaron's two sons are the measure — is the point at which the whole distribution has to be read as forward-looking, which is how Clarke and Wesley read it too.
8:
The summary verse closes the first section and repeats the warrant. Gill takes with their suburbs as the technical term it is — ground reaching two thousand cubits from the city on every side — and explains why the cities cannot be described the way tribal territories were, by their borders: they did not lie together, but stood scattered through the tribes and intermixed with their towns.

That scattering is where Gill locates the theological interest. It fulfilled Jacob's word that Levi would be divided and scattered in Israel, and it was ordered for the benefit of the tribes themselves, who would have priests and Levites at hand to instruct them in the laws and commandments of God and in all divine things. A dispersion pronounced as a judgment on Levi in Genesis 49:7 is here functioning as a means of grace to the nation.

Keil and Delitzsch move straight into the list that follows and flag the textual problem that will shadow it. There is a parallel catalogue in 1 Chronicles 6:54 and following, differently arranged, with many variations in the names and corruptions of several kinds — enough to show that the Chronicler was working from an ancient document independent of this one. The most conspicuous discrepancy is a shortfall: Chronicles names only forty-two towns, though its own totals of thirteen, ten, thirteen and twelve add to forty-eight. The names it omits are Juttah in Judah, Gibeon in Benjamin, Eltekeh and Gibbethon in Dan, and Jokneam and Nahalal in Zebulun.

Holding that in view from the start changes how the coming verses read. The list about to be given is not the only surviving form of itself, and where a name here has no counterpart there, the question of which text has suffered is open. Keil and Delitzsch will return to it, and Clarke will make a full-scale controversy of it at the end of the Merarite towns.

The list of omissions Keil and Delitzsch give is worth holding onto because it is specific: six names present here are absent from the Chronicler's roll, and yet the Chronicler's own totals require forty-eight towns. That combination — arithmetic that demands a number the names do not supply — is the mark of a text that has lost material in transmission rather than of two traditions that genuinely disagreed. The same shape of problem will reappear at the Merarite towns of Reuben, where it is this text and not Chronicles that stands accused.

Gill's reading of the dispersion deserves to be set beside Calvin's later comment, since the two arrive at the same place from opposite directions. Gill sees the scattering as the fulfilment of a word spoken against Levi and as a benefit to the tribes; Calvin will see a punishment converted into the highest honour. Neither softens what was said in Genesis, and both take the settlement described here as the point at which the judgment began to work as mercy.
9:
With the totals settled, the roll of names begins, and Gill marks the transition plainly: here follows a particular account of the several cities given out of each tribe, beginning with Judah. Keil and Delitzsch structure the section for the reader — the priests' towns in Judah and Simeon, then in Benjamin — and note that in Judah the priests received Kirjath-arba, that is Hebron, with the pasturage round about required by Numbers 35:2, while the field of the town and its villages stayed with Caleb and his family as their possession, as Joshua 14:12 had provided.

Henry uses the head of the list to say what kind of holding these towns were, and he is emphatic that it was ownership. The Levites were not tenants of the tribes in which their cities lay, with an interest that was dependent and precarious; their title was the same in kind as the title the other tribes had to their cities and lands. He argues it from the law preserving a house in a Levitical city from being alienated beyond the Jubilee, in Leviticus 25:32. He allows what Clarke argued earlier — that men of the surrounding tribe would commonly rent houses from the Levites where they could be spared, for the convenience of working the land — but that is tenancy under the Levites, not over them.

Henry then draws four observations from the shape of the list. The first is the dispersion: the Levites were scattered into all the tribes and not allowed to settle together in one district. He reads this as employment and as discipline. It found them all work and put them all at the service of others, since ministers of all people must not be idle nor live only to themselves and one another; and it kept them visible, obliged to walk as their function required, whereas living all together they would have been tempted to wink at one another's faults. He compares Christ leaving the twelve together in a body and then dispersing them to preach to every creature.

The second is that every tribe had its share, in proportion to its compass, even the most remote. All of them were God's people and therefore all had Levites among them — to receive their kindness, as Deuteronomy 12:19 and Deuteronomy 14:29 appointed, and to be consulted, so that a man who could not go up to the tabernacle might go to a Levitical city and learn the good knowledge of the LORD. Henry's image for it is a candle set in every room of the house.

The third is the size of the priests' portion, thirteen cities and some of the best, when Aaron had left only two sons — a provision made for a family the Scriptures afterwards show in very large numbers. The fourth is that several of these towns became famous otherwise: Hebron, where David began his reign; Mahanaim, where he kept his headquarters in flight from Absalom; Shechem, where Abimelech reigned. Wesley adds only that Judah and Simeon are named together because Simeon's cities lay inside Judah's portion.
10:
The verse exists to say whose the first lot was, and Gill supplies the descent: these were the children of Aaron, of the families of the Kohathites, priests because they came down from Kohath in the line of Aaron. Wesley adds a small grammatical note, that families stands in the plural for the singular, a usage he says is not unusual.

Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the head of the priestly list and run straight through what follows, and their comment is the most useful thing here because it explains a repetition that otherwise looks like a copyist's slip. They give the city of Arba, the father of Anak — that is Hebron in the hill country of Judah — with its suburbs; the fields and villages of the town go to Caleb the son of Jephunneh; and then the text says a second time that they gave to the children of Aaron Hebron with her suburbs, to be a city of refuge for the slayer, and Libnah with her suburbs. The second statement, they observe, is a repetition of the first, occasioned by the parenthetical remark about Caleb standing between them. The narrative breaks off to protect Caleb's title and then picks up its own thread.

They also begin the identifications that will run through the section, locating Libnah in the lowland at Joshua 15:42, and Jattir, Eshtemoah, Holon and Debir on the mountains of Judah at Joshua 15:48, Joshua 15:50, Joshua 15:51 and Joshua 15:49. One name they will not let stand: for Ain they read Ashan, on the authority of 1 Chronicles 6:44, placing it in the territory of Simeon at Joshua 19:7.

The precedence recorded here — theirs was the first lot — is the same fact the fourth verse gave, but stated now at the head of the names rather than in the summary of numbers, so that the list of thirteen towns begins where the lot began.

The repetition Keil and Delitzsch identify is a small thing to notice and a useful one, because it is the kind of feature that invites a charge of carelessness against the text. Read as they read it, nothing is duplicated by accident: the grant of Hebron is stated, the narrative pauses to secure Caleb's fields and villages against any inference that the priestly grant had swallowed them, and then the grant is restated so that the list of thirteen can proceed from a clean start. The parenthesis is what makes the repetition necessary.

Their correction of Ain to Ashan is the first of several places in this chapter where they prefer the Chronicler's form to the one in front of them. It is not a general preference — at the Merarite towns they will defend this text vigorously against those who would delete two of its verses — but a judgment made name by name, on the evidence of where the town can actually be placed. Ashan belongs to Simeon's territory, and the priests' portion is drawn from Judah and Simeon together.
11:
The name is given twice over, and both halves matter. Gill takes the city of Arba, the father of Anak, as the town called Kirjath-arba from him, and then reports a reading he does not invent: according to Kimchi, Anak is not a personal name at all but a general one, covering the Anakim, that race of giants among whom Arba was the chief and principal man — a prince and ruler over them, as Ben Melech has it.

Clarke does not argue the point here, referring the reader back to his note at Joshua 14:15, where the same identification of Kirjath-arba with Hebron is handled. Keil and Delitzsch, working through this stretch of the list, take the verse at face value: the city of Arba, which is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with its suburbs round about it.

What the verse does, placed where it is, is put the most storied town in Judah at the head of the priests' portion. The reading of Anak as a class rather than a man is worth registering because it changes the sense of the title: Arba is then not simply somebody's father but the head of a people, and the town that bore his name was the chief seat of the giants Israel had feared.
12:
A boundary is drawn here between two kinds of holding in the same place, and every witness who touches it treats the distinction as deliberate. Gill defines the excluded portion by measurement: the fields of the city and its villages are what lay beyond the two thousand cubits of suburb.

Clarke reads it as a protected privilege. The fields went to Caleb, and this was an exclusive grant to him and his family with which the grant to the Levites did not interfere, as he had argued at Joshua 14:14. Two titles stand in Hebron at once, and neither cancels the other.

Wesley extends the case from Hebron to the whole list, and this is the most consequential reading of the verse. Caleb's holding is not mentioned because it was peculiar to him but as an eminent instance of a rule running through every city named in the chapter: the fields and villages still belonged to the tribes from whom the cities and suburbs had been taken. He also finds a persuasive purpose in recording it here. Seeing that even Caleb gave up the town itself — though his possession had been promised long before and had just been given him by God's special command, as a mark of honour and a compensation for long and faithful service — the rest of Israel could resign a part of their possessions to the Levites the more cheerfully.
13:
The formula that opens the verse — thus they gave to the children of Aaron the priest — is the resumption Keil and Delitzsch flagged at the tenth verse, the narrative picking up after the parenthesis about Caleb's fields. Gill reads the recipients precisely: the families of the Kohathites, and within them the part that descended from Aaron and were priests.

Two things are settled by the verse as it stands. Hebron is confirmed to the priests with her suburbs and named as a city of refuge for the slayer, so that the town at the head of their portion carries the asylum function as well; and Libnah is added with her suburbs, the first of the names that follow without further comment.

Placing a city of refuge in priestly hands is not accidental to the arrangement. The man who fled there was fleeing to a town whose inhabitants served at the altar, and the chapter has already noted that Hebron came to the priests while its fields stayed with Caleb.
14:
Names follow names here with little comment attached to them, and Gill mostly refers the reader to his own earlier treatment of each town. Keil and Delitzsch carry the identification forward, reading the run of names as a single stretch: Jattir and Eshtemoa, then Holon and Debir, then Ain, Juttah and Bethshemesh, making nine cities out of the two tribes of Judah and Simeon.

Their more substantial contribution comes at the transition to Benjamin, which the same block of comment reaches. In Benjamin the priests received Gibeon, which the reader has already met in Joshua 9:3, and Geba, listed among Benjamin's towns at Joshua 18:24 — and then Anathoth and Almon, which are missing from that list of Benjamin's towns. Keil and Delitzsch flag the absence rather than smooth it over, referring back to their discussion at Joshua 18:24. Four cities from Benjamin bring the priests' total to thirteen.

The pattern is worth noticing as the list proceeds. Where a Levitical town can be matched to a name in the tribal allotments of the preceding chapters, the identification is made and the cross-reference given; where it cannot, the gap is recorded. That method is what makes the discrepancies with the parallel list in Chronicles visible instead of invisible, and it will matter a great deal when the text reaches the Merarite towns of Reuben.

Gill's habit through this stretch of referring back to his own earlier notes rather than repeating them is itself informative about the material: these are towns already described where they were first allotted, and the chapter is recording a transfer rather than introducing a place. The interest lies in which towns were chosen and from whom, not in what they were.

Anathoth and Almon are the significant pair, because their absence from Benjamin's own catalogue is not a variant reading but a silence. Keil and Delitzsch neither emend the text to supply them nor treat the earlier list as complete; they record that the two towns are missing there and point to their own discussion of the difficulty. That restraint is worth noting in a commentary quick to identify sites elsewhere, and it leaves the reader with an accurate picture of what is known.

The nine towns from Judah and Simeon and the four from Benjamin make up the thirteen the fourth verse had announced, so the priestly section closes with its arithmetic intact even where individual identifications remain open.
15:
Holon is named with her suburbs and passed over quickly; Gill sends the reader to his own earlier note on the town rather than repeating it. Keil and Delitzsch, working through this run of Judah's hill-country towns in a single comment, place Holon among the cities of the mountains of Judah listed at Joshua 15:51, alongside Jattir, Eshtemoah and Debir.

The verse is one of a sequence in which the roll simply advances. What gives it weight is its position: these are towns of the hill country going to the priests, and the identification with the earlier tribal list is what allows a reader to place them on the ground at all. Holon appears in Judah's own catalogue of possessions and reappears here as a town Judah surrendered — the same movement the chapter has been describing since the third verse, worked out one name at a time.
16:
Ain, Juttah and Bethshemesh complete the nine towns drawn from Judah and Simeon. Gill again refers to his earlier treatment of the name rather than expanding it here.

Wesley supplies the observation that makes the verse interesting. Ain and Gibeon, and some others named in this chapter, do not appear in the parallel list at 1 Chronicles 6:59. He offers two explanations and does not decide between them: either the towns were destroyed in one of the invasions that grievously wasted the land before the Chronicler wrote, or they stand in that list under other names.

The remark connects directly to what Keil and Delitzsch had said at the eighth verse about the independence of the Chronicler's document, and to their own reading of Ain as Ashan after 1 Chronicles 6:44. Where a name is missing from one of the two lists, the question is whether history or transmission accounts for it, and the witnesses here leave it open.
17:
Benjamin's contribution begins with Gibeon, and Gill's note is a single connecting thread: this is the town from which the Gibeonites came. The reader is meant to carry back the memory of Joshua 9:3 and the covenant obtained by deceit, which is why the name is not neutral when it appears in a list of priestly cities.

Geba follows with her suburbs. Keil and Delitzsch identify both towns from Benjamin's own allotment at Joshua 18:24, before noting that the two remaining Benjamite towns given to the priests are not to be found there.

The Gibeonites had been made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God, and their city is now handed to the priests who served it. The chapter does not comment on the conjunction, but it places the two facts on the same page.
18:
Anathoth carries more freight than most names in this list, and Gill loads it deliberately. He begins with a textual observation — the town is not mentioned among the cities of Benjamin in the earlier allotment — and then gives it its later fame: this was the native place of the prophet Jeremiah. On its position he assembles what he can. It lay about two or three miles north of Jerusalem, three according to Jerome; Rauwolff, travelling in those parts, describes it as a small village lying on a height; and Josephus places it within twenty furlongs of the city. Clarke's shorter note agrees on both counts, giving Anathoth as the birthplace of Jeremiah about three miles northward of Jerusalem on Jerome's authority.

Keil and Delitzsch record Almon alongside it, completing Benjamin's four, and close the priestly section with the total: all the cities of the children of Aaron were thirteen with their suburbs. They then open the next section in the same breath, the families of the Kohathites who remained receiving their towns out of Ephraim.

Their identifications for that section are worth having in view, since the verses that carry them are thin: four towns from Ephraim, four from Dan, and two from the western half of Manasseh. From Ephraim, Shechem at Joshua 17:7, Gezer at Joshua 10:33, Kibzaim — which appears as Jockmeam in 1 Chronicles 6:68, possibly another name for the same undiscovered place — and Beth-horon, without the text saying whether Upper or Lower is meant, as at Joshua 10:10. From Dan, Eltekeh and Gibbethon at Joshua 19:44, Ajalon and Gath-rimmon at Joshua 19:42 and Joshua 19:45. From half Manasseh, Taanach and a second Gath-rimmon.

The absence of Anathoth from Benjamin's own list is the same kind of gap the chapter has already shown at Gibeon and Ain. Here it happens to concern the town a major prophet came from, which is why it is the one most readers notice.

Gill's assembly of witnesses for the site of Anathoth — Jerome for the distance, Rauwolff for what the place had become by the time of his travels, Josephus for the measure in furlongs — is a compact example of how these commentators work when a name carries weight. Three independent reports are set side by side and allowed to agree, and the reader is given the evidence rather than a conclusion.

What makes the town matter is not its size. A small village on a rise a few miles north of Jerusalem is where the priest's son who would be sent to pull down and to build was raised, and the fact that this list is where Anathoth enters the priestly holdings is the reason Jeremiah is a priest at all.
19:
The priestly portion is totalled: thirteen cities with their suburbs. Gill identifies the recipients once more as those of the Kohathites who came from Aaron.

Clarke uses the total to raise the objection of scale and to answer it. At the time described here, thirteen cities were certainly too large a proportion for the priests, since they and their families amounted to a very small number. His explanation is that the provision was made with an eye to their great increase in later times, when they were organised into the twenty-four courses of David's day.

This is the same defence Keil and Delitzsch gave at the seventh verse and Wesley will give at the forty-first, arrived at independently each time and always by the same route: the grant is read as an allocation for generations rather than for a household. A distribution sized to the priests as they stood at Shiloh would have failed within a lifetime, and the text is describing a settlement meant to hold.
20:
The remaining Kohathites — those who were not priests, as Gill and Wesley both take care to say — receive their towns from Ephraim. Wesley's gloss on which remained is exactly that: over and above those who were priests.

Calvin uses the verse to explain the whole arrangement rather than this instalment of it, and his comment is the strongest theological statement in the chapter. He asks why the Levites had to be dispersed among the tribes at all, refers the reader to his commentaries on the books of Moses for the fuller treatment, and then gives the substance. The dispersion had been imposed on their progenitor as a punishment, for the cruelty and perfidy of which Levi was guilty toward the children of Shechem. But the disgrace of it had been converted into the highest honour: they were appointed a kind of guardian in every district, to hold the people to the pure worship of God.

Calvin's summary of their standing is deliberately double-edged. They were everywhere strangers — and it was with the very high dignity of acting as stewards for God, preventing their countrymen from revolting from piety. That, he says, is the reason the text states so carefully how many cities came from each tribe: they were everywhere to keep watch, and to preserve the purity of sacred rites unimpaired.
21:
Shechem heads the Kohathite towns, and Gill locates it in Mount Ephraim with a cross-reference rather than a comment. The verse itself adds what matters most: Shechem was given to be a city of refuge for the slayer, and Gezer follows with her suburbs.

Keil and Delitzsch run their identifications straight through the block that this verse opens. From Ephraim came Shechem, Gezer, Kibzaim and Beth-horon, four cities. From Dan, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Aijalon and Gath-rimmon, four more. From the half tribe of Manasseh, Taanach and Gath-rimmon, two — making ten in all for the remaining Kohathites.

Their attention then moves to the Gershonites, who received two towns from eastern Manasseh: Golan in Bashan, also a city of refuge, named at Joshua 20:8 and Deuteronomy 4:43, and Beeshterah. On that second name they do real philological work. Beeshterah is a contraction of Beth-eshterah, the house of Astarte, and it appears as Ashtaroth in 1 Chronicles 6:56. It may possibly have been the capital of King Og — the Ashtaroth-karnaim of Genesis 14:5 — or one of the two villages named Astaroth that Eusebius mentions and Jerome describes as two forts in Batanaea, nine miles apart, between the cities of Adara and Abila, though Keil and Delitzsch judge those two places too indefinite to fix the site with any exactness.

One identification they rule out flatly: the present Busra east of the Hauran cannot be meant, since that town bore its own distinct name in ancient times, attested in the Maccabean literature and in Josephus, and was afterwards corrupted into Bostra.

Shechem's designation as a city of refuge puts a third asylum town in Levitical hands, after Hebron among the priests and Golan among the Gershonites. The pattern running through the chapter is that the towns to which a manslayer could flee were towns where he would live among men whose business was the altar, and the text records the fact each time without drawing the inference.

The care Keil and Delitzsch take over Beeshterah is disproportionate to the town's importance and characteristic of their method. A contracted name is expanded, its variant in Chronicles is registered, a possible identification with Og's capital is floated and left as possible, the patristic evidence is weighed and judged too vague to fix a site, and one attractive modern identification is refused outright on the ground that the town in question demonstrably bore a different name. The result is a shorter list of certainties than a reader might want and a more reliable one.
22:
Kibzaim is the difficulty here, and Gill states it without resolving it. He suggests the town seems to be the same as Jokneam, and then concedes the harder fact: of Kibzaim under that name we read nowhere else. The name appears once, in this list, and has no independent attestation in the Hebrew Scriptures.

Beth-horon is the other town named, and Clarke raises a problem of a different kind about it. There were two cities of this name, the upper and the nether, and which is intended here cannot be ascertained. The text simply says Beth-horon with her suburbs and leaves the reader to choose.

Two names, two kinds of uncertainty — one a town that cannot be placed because it is otherwise unknown, the other a town that cannot be placed because there are two of it. Keil and Delitzsch's suggestion that Kibzaim answers to the Jockmeam of 1 Chronicles 6:68 is a proposal about the first difficulty, not a solution to it, since that place has not been discovered either.
23:
Dan's contribution opens with Eltekeh, and Gill passes it on with a cross-reference to his earlier treatment rather than a fresh note. Keil and Delitzsch place both of the towns named here in Dan's own allotment at Joshua 19:44, so that unlike Anathoth and Almon in Benjamin these names can be matched to the tribal list without difficulty.

The four towns Dan supplies to the remaining Kohathites are Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Aijalon and Gath-rimmon. Eltekeh and Gibbethon are the pair that 1 Chronicles 6:54 and following omits, one of the six absences Keil and Delitzsch catalogued when the list began — which makes the plain reading of this verse a small piece of evidence in that larger textual question.

Eltekeh is given as a city of refuge in some traditions but not so designated here; the text records it plainly with its suburbs, as it records Gibbethon beside it. Both towns lay in the coastal territory Dan had been allotted and had largely failed to hold.
24:
Aijalon and Gath-rimmon complete Dan's four. Gill refers to his earlier note on Aijalon, and Clarke does the same, pointing back to Joshua 10:12 — the valley where the moon stood still while Israel fought, which is where most readers first meet the name.

Keil and Delitzsch identify both towns from Dan's allotment, Aijalon at Joshua 19:42 and Gath-rimmon at Joshua 19:45. A second Gath-rimmon will appear two verses later among the towns of half Manasseh, and the duplication is one of the details that has drawn attention to the transmission of this list.

What the verse records is straightforward: two more towns pass from Dan to the Kohathite Levites who were not priests, with their suburbs, on the same terms as all the rest.
25:
Half Manasseh supplies two towns, Taanach and Gath-rimmon, and Gill again refers the reader to his earlier notes rather than repeating the identifications here.

Taanach is the better attested of the pair; Keil and Delitzsch place it among the towns of Manasseh in the earlier allotment. The second name is the difficulty, since Gath-rimmon has just been given as one of Dan's towns in the preceding verse. A name repeated within a few lines of a single list is the kind of feature that invites suspicion of a copying error, and it belongs with the other irregularities the commentators have been tracking — the towns missing from Benjamin's roll, the six names absent from the Chronicler's, and the two disputed verses still to come.

With these two the ten towns of the remaining Kohathites are complete.
26:
The subtotal is stated and Gill breaks it down: four out of Ephraim, four out of Dan, and two out of the half tribe of Manasseh, making the ten cities with their suburbs assigned to the families of Kohath that remained.

The arithmetic is worth pausing over because it is the second of four such totals in the chapter, and each functions as a checkpoint. Thirteen for the priests, ten for the rest of Kohath, thirteen for Gershon, twelve for Merari — the four figures were announced at the head of the chapter before any name was given, and are now being confirmed one section at a time as the names are supplied. When the confirmation fails to arrive, as it will in the Merarite section of some manuscripts, the discrepancy is immediately visible.
27:
The Gershonites receive their first towns from the eastern half of Manasseh, and Gill identifies them as the descendants of Levi's second son. The two towns are Golan in Bashan, given as a city of refuge for the slayer, and Beeshterah.

Clarke sends the reader to his fuller discussion of the asylum towns at Joshua 20:7, where the cities of refuge are treated together. Keil and Delitzsch identify Golan from Joshua 20:8 and Deuteronomy 4:43, and then give Beeshterah the extended treatment already noticed: a contraction of Beth-eshterah, the house of Astarte, appearing as Ashtaroth in 1 Chronicles 6:56.

Their handling of the possible identifications is deliberately inconclusive. Beeshterah may have been the capital of King Og, the Ashtaroth-karnaim of Genesis 14:5; or it may be one of the two places called Astaroth that Eusebius records and Jerome describes as two forts in Batanaea nine miles apart, lying between Adara and Abila. Keil and Delitzsch decline to settle it, judging those two cities too indefinite to determine the position with any exactness. The one option they exclude is Busra east of the Hauran, since that town is attested under its own quite different name in the Maccabean books and in Josephus, and was only later corrupted into Bostra.

A town whose name preserves the house of Astarte passing into the hands of Levites charged with preserving the pure worship of God is a conjunction the text records without remark, and it sits oddly beside Calvin's account of their commission at the twentieth verse.

Golan's designation as a city of refuge makes this the third asylum town to be named in the chapter and the first east of the Jordan. Clarke's practice of gathering the six into one discussion rather than treating each where it falls reflects how the law had framed them: a single institution of six towns, three on each side of the river, distributed among Levitical holdings.

Gill's identification of the Gershonites as the descendants of Levi's second son is worth setting against the order of the lots. Gershon was in fact the eldest, as Matthew Henry had noted at the head of the chapter when explaining why the younger house of Kohath was served first; Gill's ordering follows the sequence of the lots rather than of birth. The two ways of numbering the houses run through the chapter without ever being reconciled, because the lot took no account of seniority.
28:
Issachar's four towns begin with Kishon, and Gill offers a note on the name that connects it to the region's geography: the river Kishon probably took its name from the town, or the town from the river. He identifies it with the Kishion of the earlier allotment and reports that it is also called Kedesh.

Keil and Delitzsch list the four in order with their cross-references: Kishon at Joshua 19:20, Dabrath at Joshua 19:12, Jarmuth — which they equate with Remeth at Joshua 19:21 — and En-gannim, also at Joshua 19:21, appearing as Anem in 1 Chronicles 6:73.

Their comment runs on into Asher and Naphtali in the same block, and the identifications there are of a piece: Mishal or Masal, Abdon, Helkath — which stands as Hukok in 1 Chronicles 6:75, a variation they judge to be a copyist's error rather than a genuine alternative — and Rehob from Asher; Kedesh, Hammoth-dor and Kartan from Naphtali.

The pattern of double names running through this section is worth registering. Kishon and Kishion, Jarmuth and Remeth, Mishal and Masal, Helkath and Hukok, Dabareh and Dabrath: the same places are known by variant forms across the three lists, and the commentators spend their effort deciding which variants are dialect or orthography and which are corruption.

Gill's suggestion that the town and the river took their names from one another is offered as a probability and not pressed further, and he does not say which way the naming ran. The list itself is indifferent to the question; what it records is that Issachar gave the town up.

His second identification is the more difficult: that Kishion is also called Kedesh. A town of that name has already appeared in Naphtali as a city of refuge, and will appear again in this same section, so the equation asks the reader to hold two distinct places under one name. This is the ordinary hazard of the material, and it is why Keil and Delitzsch work through the parallels town by town rather than trusting a name to identify a place on its own.

The four towns from Issachar bring the Gershonite total toward its thirteen, with Asher's four and Naphtali's three still to come, and the two from eastern Manasseh already given.
29:
Jarmuth and En-gannim complete Issachar's four. Gill's note is a chain of identifications: Jarmuth is called Ramoth in one place, and is very probably the same as the Remeth of the earlier list — which is precisely the equation Keil and Delitzsch make in their own comment on the same run of towns.

Their treatment of the neighbouring tribes continues here without a break, and two of the identifications carry a judgment rather than a simple cross-reference. Helkath appearing as Hukok in Chronicles they take to be a scribal slip. Kartan they explain as a contracted form, standing for Kartain and so for Kirjathaim, comparing the way Dothan in 2 Kings 6:13 stands for the Dothain of Genesis 37:17.

On Kartan they add a caution of the kind that recurs whenever this list is compared with the tribal allotments: the town is not mentioned among Naphtali's cities at Joshua 19:33 and following. They report Knobel's suggestion that it may be Katanah, a ruined site north-east of Safed, and attribute the identification to him rather than adopting it.

The section is a dense piece of topographical work, and its usefulness lies less in any single identification than in the consistency of the method: name the town, give its place in the earlier allotment where it has one, note where it has none, and mark the variants without pretending they are all resolvable.

Gill's chain of names for a single town — Jarmuth here, Ramoth in one place, Remeth in another — is a compact illustration of what makes this section laborious. Three forms, one site, and the identification resting on position in parallel lists rather than on the forms themselves.

En-gannim, the fourth of Issachar's towns, appears as Anem in the Chronicler's roll, which is a fourth instance of the same phenomenon within a few verses. Keil and Delitzsch record each variation as they meet it and reserve the word error for cases where a form cannot be explained as a legitimate variant, as they do with Hukok for Helkath.

Their willingness to attribute a suggestion to Knobel rather than absorb it is characteristic of the commentary's manner. A proposed identification of Kartan with a ruined site north-east of Safed is reported with its author's name attached, which leaves the reader able to weigh it as a conjecture rather than receive it as a finding.
30:
Asher's contribution opens with Mishal, and Gill gives the variants rather than a description: the same town appears as Misheal in the earlier allotment and as Mashal elsewhere. Abdon is named with it.

Keil and Delitzsch place Mishal or Masal at Joshua 19:26 and compare the form in 1 Chronicles 6:74, and Abdon at Joshua 19:28. Both towns can be matched to Asher's own catalogue, so this pair raises none of the difficulties that Anathoth or Kartan raise.

The three-fold variation in the first name — Mishal, Misheal, Mashal — is the ordinary texture of this material. What changes across the lists is spelling and vocalisation rather than the place itself.

Gill gives no further description of either town, and Keil and Delitzsch add only the cross-references. That the Gershonites, descended from Levi's firstborn, drew the more distant tribes is a feature of the lot rather than of any precedence among the houses, as the ordering of the four allotments has shown throughout.
31:
Helkath and Rehob complete Asher's four, and Gill notes at once that Helkath is the town appearing as Hukok in the parallel list.

Keil and Delitzsch, working through the same block, treat that difference as an error rather than a variant, and place Helkath at Joshua 19:25 and Rehob at Joshua 19:28 in Asher's allotment. They then move to Naphtali's three — Kedesh in Galilee, named at Joshua 19:37 and Joshua 12:22 and given here as a city of refuge; Hammoth-dor, which stands as Hammath at Joshua 19:35 and as Hammon in 1 Chronicles 6:76; and Kartan, explained as a contraction for Kirjathaim.

The section closes with the Gershonite total of thirteen towns, and then opens the Merarite portion: from Zebulun, Jokneam and Kartah. Keil and Delitzsch identify Jokneam from Joshua 19:11 and Joshua 12:22, and flag Kartah and Dimnah as names absent from Zebulun's own list and otherwise unknown. On Dimnah they record and reject a common identification: many commentators equate it with the Rimmono of 1 Chronicles 6:77, but they judge the reason insufficient, since the Chronicler's text is corrupt at that point, giving only two names where four are required.

The Gershonite thirteen are now complete: two from eastern Manasseh, four from Issachar, four from Asher, and three from Naphtali. Each subtotal has matched the figure announced at the head of the chapter, which is what makes the coming failure of the Merarite arithmetic conspicuous rather than easy to miss.

Keil and Delitzsch's treatment of Kartan as a contraction is a small piece of philology with a practical use. Read as a shortened Kirjathaim, the name becomes searchable in other lists; read as it stands, it is a place mentioned once and nowhere else. The comparison they draw with Dothan and Dothain shows the contraction is a known pattern in Hebrew place-names rather than an expedient invented for this verse.

Their scepticism about Rimmono, on the other hand, runs the other way — a proposed identification refused because the text that would supply it is demonstrably defective at that point. The two judgments together show the method is not simply a preference for harmonising names.
32:
Naphtali gives three towns, and the first is Kedesh in Galilee, named here as a city of refuge for the slayer. Gill refers the reader to his earlier notes on the place.

This is the fifth of the six asylum towns to appear in the chapter, after Hebron, Shechem, Golan and — in the disputed verses still to come — Bezer, with Ramoth in Gilead following. All six fall to Levites, and the chapter records the fact town by town as it reaches each of them rather than stating it as a rule.

Hammoth-dor and Kartan complete Naphtali's three. Keil and Delitzsch identify Kedesh from Joshua 19:37, treat Hammoth-dor as the Hammath of Joshua 19:35, and explain Kartan as a contracted form of Kirjathaim which does not appear in Naphtali's own list at all.
33:
The Gershonite total is given: thirteen cities with their suburbs, divided among the families according to their number, as Gill notes.

Keil and Delitzsch confirm the figure and pass directly into the Merarite section, which is where the chapter's principal textual difficulty lies. The Merarites received twelve towns. From Zebulun came four — Jokneam, identified from Joshua 19:11 and Joshua 12:22; Kartah and Dimnah, neither of which appears among Zebulun's towns at Joshua 19:11 and following, and neither of which is otherwise known; and Nahalal at Joshua 19:15.

On Dimnah they enter a note of dissent from a widely held identification. Many commentators take Dimnah to be the Rimmono of 1 Chronicles 6:77, but Keil and Delitzsch hold that the Chronicler's text is corrupt at that point — it supplies only two names, Rimmono and Tabor, where four are needed — so the equation rests on a passage that cannot bear it.

Reuben's four follow: Bezer, itself a city of refuge under Deuteronomy 4:43, together with Jahza, Kedemoth and Mephaath, the last three identified from Joshua 13:18. Those four towns are the subject of the controversy that Clarke will set out at length two verses further on, since the verses naming them are precisely the ones some authorities would delete.

The verse is a subtotal and nothing more, but it stands at the seam of the chapter. Everything before it has confirmed the figures announced at the fourth to seventh verses; everything after it belongs to the section where, in some copies, the figures fail.

Keil and Delitzsch's note on Dimnah is placed here because their comment runs continuously across the seam, and it repays attention as a piece of critical practice. The identification with Rimmono is not rejected because it is implausible in itself but because the verse that would supply it has manifestly lost material — two names standing where four are required. A corrupt witness cannot be used to identify a doubtful name, however attractive the resemblance.

The Merarite towns from Zebulun therefore arrive with two of their four unidentifiable, and the Reubenite four that follow arrive under a question about whether their verses belong to the text at all.
34:
Merari is introduced as Gill has introduced each house in turn — the descendants of Levi's youngest son, and all that remained of the Levites still unprovided with cities. The first towns come from Zebulun: Jokneam and Kartah with their suburbs.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the identifications and the gaps together. Jokneam is placed from Joshua 19:11 and Joshua 12:22. Kartah and Dimnah are not among Zebulun's towns in the earlier allotment and are unknown from any other source. Nahalal is placed from Joshua 19:15, completing the four.

Their footnote on Dimnah repeats the caution against identifying it with the Chronicler's Rimmono, on the ground that the parallel passage is corrupt where it would have to be sound. It is a small point in itself, but it shows the principle they apply throughout the section: a variant is only useful for identification if the text carrying it can be trusted at that place, and here it cannot.

The comment then runs ahead to Reuben's four towns, Bezer, Jahza, Kedemoth and Mephaath, and to the note on the manuscript history that will occupy the next two verses. That the Merarite section carries both the largest number of unidentifiable names and the chapter's one genuine textual controversy is not a coincidence; these are the towns furthest from the centre and the least often mentioned elsewhere.

Gill's phrase for the Merarites — all that remained of the Levites unprovided of cities — describes the last stage of a distribution that has been working outward from the sanctuary since the fourth verse. The priests took the towns nearest the future temple, the remaining Kohathites the ring beyond them, the Gershonites the north, and Merari what was left: Zebulun in the north, and Reuben and Gad across the Jordan.

Jokneam is the one Zebulunite town that can be placed with confidence, appearing both in Zebulun's own allotment and among the kings Joshua defeated. Kartah and Dimnah cannot be placed at all, and Nahalal returns the section to solid ground.

The proportion of unidentifiable names rises sharply in this final section, and there is a plain reason for it. These are the towns least often mentioned in the later history, in the territories most exposed and earliest lost, and a place-name survives in the record largely by being mentioned again.
35:
Dimnah and Nahalal close Zebulun's four, and with them the chapter reaches its one substantial dispute about the text itself. Gill notes only that Dimnah is nowhere else mentioned, unless it be the same as Rimmon.

Clarke states the problem in its bibliographical form. It is well known to every Hebrew scholar, he writes, that the two verses following are wholly omitted by the Masora and are left out of some of the most correct and authentic Hebrew Bibles; and among critics there is no small controversy about their authenticity. He directs those who want the arguments at length to De Rossi's collection of variant readings.

Clarke then gives Kennicott's case for keeping them, and it is an argument from arithmetic rather than from manuscripts. The chapter states that the Levitical cities were forty-eight and that all of them have been described, so all of them must be specified here. Yet in Hebrew copies printed in full obedience to the Masora — which excludes two verses containing four cities — the names amount to only forty-four. Working through the sections, thirteen are named for the priests, ten for the remaining Kohathites, thirteen for Gershon, and then four and four for Merari: forty-four in all. Worse, the closing verse of the Merarite section infers a total of twelve from the verses immediately preceding, which without the disputed pair supply only eight.

On that reasoning the two verses were inserted in the earliest printed editions of the Hebrew text and stand in Walton's Polyglot and in the English Bible; and Kennicott reports one hundred and forty-nine copies preserving them. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by a different route, judging the omission a copyist's error occasioned by similar line-endings, and observing that the verses appear in many good manuscripts and old editions earlier than 1525 and in all the ancient versions.

Clarke's own verdict is more guarded than Kennicott's. Though the reasoning appears conclusive, he says, the variations among the manuscripts that retain the verses and those that reject them are so many and so important as to make the question very difficult to determine. He adds that those who deny their authenticity hold them to have been imported from 1 Chronicles 6:78 and following, where they are found in general but not exactly as they stand here — and he notes that upwards of forty further manuscripts collated by De Rossi may be added to Kennicott's total.
36:
This is the first of the two verses whose place in the text Clarke has just laid out at length. It names Bezer with her suburbs and Jahazah with her suburbs, from the tribe of Reuben.

Gill supplies the detail that matters most for the arithmetic: Bezer was a city of refuge, and the fifth of them in this account, though the fact is not remarked here as it is at Hebron, Shechem, Golan and Kedesh. He notes that the Greek version does mark it. Clarke, for his part, refers the reader to his earlier note on Jahazah at Joshua 13:18.

The observation about Bezer is quietly decisive in the textual argument. If these verses are removed, the chapter loses not only four towns but one of the six cities of refuge, which Deuteronomy 4:43 names among Reuben's possessions. A list of Levitical towns that omitted an asylum town assigned by name in the law would be defective on its face.
37:
Kedemoth and Mephaath complete Reuben's four, and Gill notes that a wilderness of the same name lay near Kedemoth.

Keil and Delitzsch pass on to Gad's four: Ramoth in Gilead, given as a city of refuge, and Mahanaim, both identified from Joshua 13:26; then Heshbon from Joshua 13:17 and Jaezer from Joshua 13:25, with a cross-reference to Numbers 21:32. That makes twelve for Merari when the Reubenite towns are counted, which is the figure the section's closing verse requires.

Their comment then reaches the summary that ends the whole catalogue, and they pause on its phrasing. The text says the cities were every one with their suburbs round about them, and the Hebrew repeats the word for city — city by city — which they gloss as meaning every city, each with its pasture around it. The repetition is distributive rather than emphatic, and it closes the list by asserting of each town individually what has been said of them collectively throughout.

With that the roll of forty-eight is complete, and the chapter turns from the towns to the wider claim about the land which the last three verses make.

Kedemoth gives its name to a wilderness lying near it, as Gill notes, and Mephaath completes Reuben's four — and with them the disputed pair of verses closes.

Gad's four follow immediately, and two of them are among the better-known towns east of the Jordan. Ramoth in Gilead is named here as a city of refuge, the sixth and last of them. Mahanaim is the town Matthew Henry had noted as David's headquarters in flight from Absalom.

Heshbon's inclusion among Gad's towns is the detail Gill will take up at the next verse, since the city had belonged to Reuben by the earlier allotment. Jaezer, the fourth, is identified from the same stretch of Joshua 13:1 onward and from the account of its capture in Numbers 21:32.

The distributive phrasing of the summary — every city with its own pasture round about it — closes the catalogue on the same note the third verse opened it. What Israel granted was never bare title to a name on a list but a town with ground enough to keep the cattle that were the Levites' only stock, and the text asserts it of each of the forty-eight in turn.
38:
Gad's towns are introduced, and Gill's note fixes their position rather than their identity: this tribe, like Reuben, lay on the other side of Jordan.

The two named here are Ramoth in Gilead, given as a city of refuge for the slayer, and Mahanaim. Matthew Henry had already picked Mahanaim out at the head of the list as one of the Levitical towns that became famous on other grounds, being where David lay and kept his headquarters when he fled from Absalom.

With Ramoth the six cities of refuge are complete: three west of the Jordan at Hebron, Shechem and Kedesh, and three east at Bezer, Ramoth and Golan. Every one of them has fallen to Levites in the course of this chapter.
39:
Heshbon and Jazer complete Gad's four. Gill gives Heshbon its history: it had been the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites, and was first given to the Reubenites and rebuilt by them, but stood on the border of Gad and appears from this verse to have become one of Gad's towns.

Keil and Delitzsch record the four and then the Merarite total of twelve, and move into the closing summary of the whole list — forty-eight cities of the Levites within the possession of the children of Israel, every one with its suburbs round about it.

They then mark the structural point that governs the last three verses of the chapter. The closing paragraph forms the conclusion not merely to this chapter but to the whole account of the division of the land running from Joshua 13:1 onward, pointing back to Joshua 11:23 and further back still to Joshua 1:2, and so joining the two halves of the book together. By the division of Canaan among the tribes, the promise Joshua had received after the death of Moses was fulfilled: the LORD had given Israel the whole land he had sworn to the fathers in Genesis 12:7 and Genesis 15:18, and they had taken possession of it to dwell in.

A royal Amorite capital ending its history as a Levitical town on a tribal border is a fair emblem of what the chapter has been recording. The list began with a petition and ends with the possession of a land, and the towns in between changed hands by lot.

Gill's account of Heshbon carries the whole history of the place in a sentence. It had been Sihon's royal city; it passed to Reuben, who rebuilt it; and it stood on the border, so that this verse reads as evidence that it had come to be counted among Gad's towns. Nothing in the chapter explains the transfer, and Gill infers it from the list rather than asserting it.

The structural observation Keil and Delitzsch make here is the most consequential thing in the closing verses. The paragraph beginning at the forty-third verse is not the end of a chapter about Levitical cities but the end of the entire account of the division that began at Joshua 13:1, reaching back past Joshua 11:23 to the commission given after Moses died. The book's two halves — conquest and division — are joined at this point, and what follows about the land and the promise is the conclusion of both.
40:
The Merarite total closes the fourth and last section: twelve cities. Gill notes that they were distributed by lot according to the number of the families, and were sufficient for them.

The figure is the one that made the textual controversy visible. Twelve is what this verse infers from the towns immediately preceding, and the towns immediately preceding supply twelve only if the two disputed verses naming Reuben's four are read as part of the text. Where they are omitted the section yields eight, and the summary contradicts the list it summarises.

Keil and Delitzsch record the total without hesitation, having already judged the omission to be a copyist's error. The arithmetic here is the strongest single argument on that side of the question.
41:
The grand total is given — forty-eight cities with their suburbs, within the possession of the children of Israel — and Gill notes simply that it comprises the four sections in one sum.

Clarke returns at this point to the objection he raised at the priests' thirteen, now in its fullest form. At the last census the tribe of Levi amounted to only twenty-three thousand, and forty-eight cities is supposed by some too great a proportion for so small a tribe when the others have so few. He answers in six parts: not all the cities of the other tribes are enumerated; those tribes had the surrounding country as well as their towns; the Levites had no cities beyond those listed; they had no land annexed to their cities beyond the two thousand cubits for their cattle; cities in those ancient times were very small, most villages going under that name; and the Levites had now the appointment suited to their later increase. He adds a reason of principle: the other tribes might enlarge their borders by conquest, which was not suitable to the mere servants of God, since conquest would have made them proprietors of land, and God had determined they should have no inheritance in Israel, being himself their portion.

Calvin turns the same figure into an argument about the rest of the book. This passage more than any other shows what he has repeatedly urged, that the boundaries of the other tribes were not so confined as to comprehend no more cities than are actually named. Levi was the least numerous of all the tribes; with what equity could it have been allowed to expand over four times the space allowed to Zebulun, which though more populous is mentioned as possessing only twelve cities? Sixteen are enumerated for Issachar, nineteen for Naphtali, twenty-two for Asher. It would have been an unequal division to give the greater number of cities to the smaller population. He infers that many cities went unmentioned, and that the extent of Levi's lot makes plain how large the other territories must have been.

Wesley's answer covers the same ground in three parts and adds one of his own. It does not appear the Levites had more, since all their cities are expressed while many of the others' are omitted. The Levites were confined to their cities and suburbs, whereas the rest had large territories they could improve, so one of their cities might be worth several of the Levites'. And God was pleased to deal liberally with his ministers, to put honour on those whom he foresaw many would be prone to despise, and so that being free from outward distractions they might devote themselves the more entirely to his service.
42:
The closing formula of the catalogue states of every town individually what has been said of the list as a whole. Gill takes the suburbs at their legal measure: a space reaching two thousand cubits on every side, assigned to each of the cities named, for keeping their cattle and laying up provision for them.

Keil and Delitzsch had drawn attention to the Hebrew idiom here, the word for city repeated so as to mean city by city, each with its pasture round about. The construction is distributive, and it closes the roll by making the grant particular rather than general.

The verse is the last of the list. What follows belongs to a different scale of statement altogether, and the transition is abrupt: from the measured ground outside forty-eight towns to the whole land sworn to the fathers.
43:
Three verses close the entire account of the division, and the first of them makes the largest claim in the book. Gill reads it with care about what gave means: the land was all given them by lot, whether subdued or not, and the greater part was actually put into their hands — as much as they could for the present occupy and cultivate — while such parts as remained in Canaanite hands were subject to tribute. That more was not possessed later he attributes to Israel's own sloth, adding that it was in any case God's will that the enemy be driven out by little and little, until Israel had increased enough to occupy the whole, lest the land lie waste and the wild beasts multiply.

Henry treats the paragraph as the conclusion of the whole history, set against the promise so that each illuminates the other: the performance makes the promise appear very true, and the promise makes the performance appear very kind. God had promised Abraham's seed the land of Canaan, and now at last they possessed it and dwelt in it — though they had often forfeited the benefit and God had long delayed. Henry draws the parallel he cannot resist: the promise of the heavenly Canaan is as sure to all God's spiritual Israel, being the promise of him that cannot lie.

Clarke presses the historical case and then answers a standing objection. All was now divided by lot, their enemies so completely discomfited that no army remained to make head against them; those left in the land served under tribute, and the tribute itself was proof of subjugation. Israel had as much in actual possession as they could occupy, and as they increased God enabled them to drive out the rest — though their infidelity later let their enemies straiten them. He insists that God never promised to give or maintain them in the land except on condition of obedience, and that there is not a single instance on record of their being straitened or subjugated while faithful. The cavil that they never possessed the whole and therefore the promise was not divine he calls as foolish as it is unprincipled, and answers it with an analogy from his own day: a territory held under tribute is a territory conquered, whatever the composition of its population.

Calvin takes the harder form of the difficulty and states it against himself. How can Israel be said to have been settled in possession, and not one syllable of God's promises to have failed, when many of the enemy remained intermingled with them, when the divine intention was that none should be left, and when Israel not only failed to drive them out but admitted them as neighbours and made pacts with them? His resolution is to distinguish two things that the objection runs together: the certain, clear and steadfast faithfulness of God in keeping his promises, and the effeminacy and sluggishness of the people, through which the benefit of that goodness in a manner slipped through their hands. Whatever war they undertook, in whatever direction they moved their standards, victory was prepared; the only obstacle to exterminating their enemies was their own voluntary torpor. So the truth of God came visibly forth even where the possession was not made clear, since what remained might have been obtained without difficulty had they cared to take the victories offered them.
44:
Rest is the second term of the promise, and Gill defines it by what it ended: not only their travels, forty years of them, but the wars with the Canaanites they had been engaged in for some years past.

Henry lists the same rest in its parts — rest from the fatigue of the wilderness march, which he supposes was long in their bones; rest from their wars in Canaan; and rest from the insults their enemies had first offered them. They dwelt now not merely in habitations of their own but in quiet and peaceable ones, and though Canaanites remained, none had the strength or spirit to attack them or even to raise an alarm. His qualification is sharp and characteristic: this rest continued until they, by their own sin and folly, put thorns into their own beds and their own eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the wording rather than the experience. The expression points back to Deuteronomy 12:9 and refers to all the promises of the Pentateuch that assured Israel of peaceable possession, such as Exodus 33:14 and Deuteronomy 3:20. No enemy had been able to withstand them, as the LORD had promised Joshua at Joshua 1:5. They allow the obvious fact that the Canaanites were not exterminated, and explain the claim accordingly: those left had become so powerless that they could neither accomplish nor attempt anything against Israel — so long as Israel adhered faithfully to God, or so long as Joshua and the elders of his generation were alive, as Judges 2:6 and following makes plain.

Wesley compresses the whole qualification into a clause. God gave them rest, namely all the days of Joshua; for afterwards it was otherwise with them. The three witnesses agree that the verse is true as written and true of a period, and none of them reads it as a permanent condition.

The three readings of the verse fit together rather than compete. Gill defines the rest by the two things it ended, Henry describes what it felt like to the generation that received it, Keil and Delitzsch trace which promises it fulfils, and Wesley marks how long it lasted.

Only the last of these introduces a limit, and it is a limit the text itself supplies elsewhere rather than an inference from later disappointment. The rest is real, complete, and bounded by the lifetime of the men who had seen the work done — which is exactly how Judges 2:6 and following describes the transition to what came next.
45:
The last verse of the section is an unqualified statement, and every witness handles it by asking what it can bear. Gill reads the emphasis in the doubled phrasing: not only every good thing in general but every part and particular of that good thing, with all that was included in it or appended to it.

Henry hears in it a testimony subscribed by Israel and made again by Solomon at 1 Kings 8:56, with all Israel in effect saying amen to it. His summary of the whole matter is that the inviolable truth of God's promise, and its performance to the utmost, are what all the saints have been ready to bear witness to; and that where the performance has seemed to come short, they have been equally ready to own that the blame lies with themselves. He applies the same distinction to the Canaanites who remained. Their presence now was no contradiction of the promise, since God had said in Exodus 23:30 that he would drive them out by little and little rather than at once; Israel had as much as they had hands to manage, and the rest were holding uncultivated country against the beasts of the field. Their later prevalence was another matter — the effect of Israel's cowardice and sloth, and the punishment of a sinful inclination to the abominations of the heathen whom they harboured and indulged.

Keil and Delitzsch put the same reading in exact terms. Of all the good words the LORD had spoken, not one had fallen — that is, remained unfulfilled — but all had come to pass. The phrase relates to the promises about peaceful possession of Canaan, which were the basis of all the salvation promised to Israel and the pledge that the remaining promises would be kept. Notwithstanding that much country still remained in Canaanite hands, the promise of the land had been fulfilled, since God had never promised immediate and total destruction of the Canaanites but only their gradual extermination, as Exodus 23:29 and Deuteronomy 7:22 had said. They add the honest limit: Israel never came into undisputed possession of the whole land to the full boundaries laid down in Numbers 34:1 and following, never conquering Tyre and Sidon.

Wesley ends where Henry ends, on the testimony rather than the survey. The inviolable truth of God's promise and its performance to the uttermost is what all believers in Christ have always been ready to testify; and where anything has seemed to come short, they have been as ready to take the blame upon themselves.
